IndusEquip Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusEquip Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson (Vice President of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusEquip Inc.'s results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today's call are Alex Harper, Chief Executive Officer; Jennifer Lee, Chief Financial Officer; Mark Rodriguez, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Sofia Chen, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Harper.

Alex Harper (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusEquip Inc.'s performance for the Q3 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering strong results amid a resilient industrial environment marked by infrastructure tailwinds and our strategic focus on high-margin digital services. Key highlights include our robust operating margin expansion across segments, fueled by favorable mix shifts and productivity gains; explosive growth in automation and digital offerings, which boosted efficiency and recurring revenue; effective cost reduction programs that enhanced profitability; solid backlog conversion supporting revenue momentum; a commitment to shareholder returns through our progressive dividend policy; and meaningful advancements in our Industry 4.0 platforms like IndusEdge AI. These efforts underscore our positioning for sustained growth in capital equipment, aftermarket parts, and services.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Jennifer Lee to provide more detail on our financial results.

Jennifer Lee (CFO):
Thank you, Alex. Turning to our financial performance, IndusEquip Inc. reported $1.48 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 28.5%, driven by improved product mix—particularly in servo-driven CNC machining centers and IoT-enabled predictive maintenance contracts—along with disciplined pricing and supply chain efficiencies. Operating expenses were $120 million, resulting in an operating income of $220 million. Our net income for the quarter was $165 million, or $1.25 per share.

Good afternoon, everyone—thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. As we review these results, I'd like to dive deeper into our operating margin performance by segment, which came in strong at 15.4% overall—up 210 basis points year-over-year and 80 basis points sequentially from Q2. This marks our best quarterly margin in three years, driven by a favorable product mix shift toward high-margin automation and aftermarket services, disciplined pricing actions averaging 4.2% across the portfolio, and productivity gains from our Enterprise Lean Sigma program, which delivered $28 million in bottom-line benefits this quarter alone.

Let me break it down by our four core segments: Industrial Automation, Heavy Machinery, Precision Components, and Aftermarket Services, highlighting key drivers, trends, regional nuances, and the strategic levers we're pulling to sustain this momentum in a market still grappling with steel price volatility—up 12% YoY per S&P Global data—and lingering supply chain headwinds from Red Sea disruptions.

In the Industrial Automation segment, revenue grew 18% to $420 million, with operating margins expanding to 22.1% from 19.3% a year ago—a 280 bps improvement. This segment, which includes our PLCs, SCADA systems, and collaborative robots akin to those from Rockwell Automation or Fanuc, benefited from robust demand in factory floor digitalization. Capacity utilization hit 92%, up from 85% last year, thanks to our $50 million investment in a new brownfield MES upgrade in our Milwaukee facility, boosting throughput by 15%. Regionally, North America drove 60% of growth with margins at 24%, fueled by reshoring trends—U.S. onshoring initiatives added $45 million in orders from EV battery gigafactories. EMEA margins dipped to 19% due to energy surcharges in Germany amid the nuclear phase-out, but we're mitigating with our Edge AI predictive maintenance suite, which reduced unplanned downtime by 28% for customers like Siemens-partnered OEMs. APAC was stellar at 23% margins, with China bookings up 25% on semiconductor fab expansions, though we're hedging tariff risks via localized production in Vietnam. Strategically, we're accelerating our 'Automation 4.0' roadmap, targeting 25% margins by FY25 through software margins north of 80% on recurring revenue streams.

In Heavy Machinery, revenue was flat at $580 million, but margins rebounded sharply to 13.8% from 9.5% YoY—440 bps of expansion. Our excavators, wheel loaders, and hydraulic presses—competitive with Caterpillar's 320 series or Komatsu's PC lineup—faced softer volumes amid high interest rates crimping capex in mining and construction. However, we clawed back profitability via 5.8% pricing, lower COGS as aluminum spot prices stabilized post-Ukraine supply shocks, and a 10% reduction in warranty costs from our Gen-3 hydraulic sealing tech. North America margins led at 15.2%, supported by infrastructure bill tailwinds—$120 million backlog from data center site prep. Europe lagged at 11% due to weak German infra spend and 20% YoY diesel cost inflation, prompting us to idle 15% of underutilized capacity in our Dortmund plant while ramping U.S. output. APAC margins hit 14.5%, with India offsetting China construction slowdowns via rural road projects. Looking ahead, our pivot to hybrid-electric drivetrains—mirroring Deere's sustainability push—positions us for 16% margins next year, with EPA-compliant models already winning 30% market share in California fleets.

Precision Components saw revenue decline 5% to $310 million, reflecting destocking in aero aftermarket channels, but margins held resilient at 12.4% versus 11.2% last year—120 bps uptick. This segment's CNC-machined gears, turbine blades, and forgings for OEMs like GE Aviation and Boeing faced titanium pricing pressures, up 8% on Russian export curbs. Yet, our digital twin simulation tech cut scrap rates by 22%, and selective surcharges preserved mix. Regionally, North America was rock-solid at 14%, buoyed by F-35 program ramps and SpaceX supplier quals adding $25 million. EMEA slipped to 10.5% from Airbus A320neo delays, but our AS9100D recertification opened doors for next-gen hydrogen turbine components. APAC grew margins to 13% via aerospace offsets in South Korea's KFX fighter program. Strategically, we're deploying Industry 4.0 cobots from our automation segment internally, aiming for sub-10% COGS as a percentage of sales by optimizing our Ohio precision fab for reshored semiconductor wafer handling tools.

The Aftermarket Services segment was the star performer: revenue up 22% to $290 million, margins soaring to 28.6% from 25.4%—320 bps expansion. Parts, remanufacturing, and field services for our installed base of 1.2 million machines generated 65% recurring revenue, insulating us from OEM cyclicality. IoT-enabled predictive analytics—our 'IndusGuard' platform, similar to Honeywell's Forge—drove a 35% uptake in service contracts, with uptime guarantees yielding 18% pricing power. North America dominated at 30% margins, with mining fleet upgrades in Nevada. EMEA held at 27% despite UK steel recyc costs, while APAC exploded to 29% on Indonesian palm oil processor modernizations. Our strategy here is clear: cross-selling digital services into our 85% attach rate target, leveraging a $2.1 billion backlog to deliver 30%+ margins long-term.

Overall insights: Excluding a $12 million one-time restructuring gain, adjusted operating margins were 14.9%, still up 190 bps YoY. SG&A leverage improved to 9.2% of sales from 10.1%, and inventory turns rose to 5.2x amid disciplined working capital management. Challenges persist—labor tightness in U.S. skilled trades pushed wages up 6%, and we're monitoring U.S.-China trade rhetoric impacting 15% of components. But our book-to-bill of 1.25x and $4.8 billion backlog provide visibility. We're on track for full-year margins of 15-16%, with bolt-on M&A in automation software and capex at $220 million focused on U.S. and Mexico for nearshoring. This positions IndusEquip to outperform peers like Parker Hannifin or Illinois Tool Works in a recovering industrial cycle.

Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. As we review our Q3 results, I'd like to dive deeper into our cost reduction initiatives, which have been a cornerstone of delivering the robust profitability we reported today. In an industry facing persistent inflationary pressures on raw materials like steel and aluminum—up 15% year-over-year globally, per S&P Global data—and supply chain disruptions reminiscent of the 2021 semiconductor shortages that hammered OEMs like Caterpillar and John Deere, our disciplined approach has driven gross margin expansion of 320 basis points to 28.4%, and adjusted EBITDA margins up 450 basis points to 22.1%. These aren't one-off gains; they're the result of a multi-pronged strategy yielding over $185 million in run-rate savings annualized, with more to come.

Breaking it down by key pillars, supply chain optimization accounted for 45% of our savings, or roughly $83 million. We've aggressively consolidated our supplier base from over 1,200 to 850 strategic partners, focusing on long-term contracts with volume discounts averaging 8-12%. For instance, in our hydraulic systems division—critical for heavy equipment like excavators and presses—we renegotiated with key steel providers in the U.S. Midwest, locking in Q4 pricing at $850 per ton versus the spot market's $1,050. This mirrors moves by peers like Parker Hannifin, but we've gone further by reshoring 25% of our castings production from China to Mexico and our new facility in Ohio. This not only mitigated U.S.-China tariffs, which added 10-15% to landed costs last year, but also reduced lead times by 35% and freight expenses by $22 million. Regionally, this has been particularly accretive in North America, where truckload rates stabilized post-2022 peaks, contributing to a 5% sequential drop in COGS per unit.

Operational efficiency and lean manufacturing initiatives delivered $52 million in savings, or 28% of the total. We've rolled out Kaizen events across all 14 global plants, targeting waste elimination in line with Toyota Production System principles adapted for our CNC machining and assembly lines. A standout example is our adoption of value stream mapping at the Spartanburg facility, where we've cut changeover times on our modular conveyor systems—used in automotive assembly for clients like Ford and GM—from 4 hours to 45 minutes, boosting throughput by 22%. This directly flowed through to inventory turns improving from 4.2x to 5.8x, freeing up $45 million in working capital. In Europe, where energy costs surged 40% due to the Ukraine conflict, we've implemented energy management systems, reducing natural gas consumption by 18% via variable frequency drives on our welding robots. This shaved €12 million off OpEx in the region, helping offset softer demand in industrial machinery amid the Eurozone slowdown.

Automation and digital transformation represent the highest-ROI pillar, contributing $35 million or 19% of savings, with CapEx payback under 18 months. We've invested $120 million over the past 12 months in Industry 4.0 technologies, including 150 collaborative robots (cobots) from partners like Universal Robots and AI-driven predictive maintenance via Siemens MindSphere. In our power transmission gear segment—think gearboxes for wind turbines and mining conveyors—machine learning algorithms have reduced unplanned downtime by 42%, from 7% to 4.1% of available hours. This is especially vital in Asia-Pacific, where we've localized production in India to serve the booming infrastructure market; our Pune plant now runs 24/7 with digital twins simulating 95% of failure modes, cutting scrap rates on aluminum extrusions by 15%. Compared to Ingersoll Rand's recent automation push, ours is more integrated, linking ERP with IoT for real-time COGS visibility.

SG&A and overhead rationalization rounded out the program with $15 million in savings. We've right-sized our global workforce by 8%, or 1,200 positions, through attrition and retraining into higher-value roles like data analysts for our supply chain AI platform. Travel and facilities costs dropped 22% via virtual collaboration tools, and we've outsourced non-core IT to Infosys, saving $8 million annually. Importantly, these moves haven't compromised safety or quality—our Total Recordable Incident Rate remains at 0.9, below the industry average of 1.5 per OSHA benchmarks.

Turning to the profitability impact: These initiatives have transformed our P&L. Q3 COGS as a percentage of sales fell 410 basis points year-over-year to 71.6%, driven by the levers I described. Adjusted gross profit hit $285 million, up 14% sequentially, while EBITDA reached a record $148 million—12% ahead of consensus—yielding that 22.1% margin. Free cash flow conversion exceeded 110% of EBITDA, funding $75 million in share repurchases and a 10% dividend hike. Segment-wise, our Industrial Equipment segment saw EBITDA margins expand 520 basis points to 24.3%, fueled by pricing discipline (up 4.2% average) and mix shift toward high-margin aftermarket parts, now 32% of revenue.

Strategically, this positions us exceptionally well in the Manufacturing/Industrial Equipment space. With global CapEx cycles turning up—McKinsey forecasts 5-7% CAGR through 2027 on reshoring and electrification—we're leveraging these efficiencies to gain share against slower adapters like legacy players in hydraulic valves. Sustainability ties in too: our initiatives cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 22%, aligning with EU CBAM tariffs and customer ESG mandates from the likes of Siemens and GE Vernova. Looking forward, we see another $100 million in run-rate savings by year-end 2025, targeting 25%+ EBITDA margins, with 60% from scaling digital tools enterprise-wide.

Before we move to operations, let me address our dividend policy and yield, as this remains a cornerstone of our capital return framework here at IndusEquip. Our board today declared a quarterly dividend of $0.68 per share, payable December 15th to shareholders of record as of November 25th. That's a 6% increase over the prior quarter's payout, marking our 28th consecutive annual dividend hike. On an annualized basis, this brings our dividend to $2.72 per share, delivering a forward yield of approximately 2.9% at yesterday's closing price of $93.50. For context, that's comfortably above the S&P 500 Industrials sector average of 2.1% and in line with Dividend Aristocrats like Emerson Electric and Dover Corporation, reflecting our blue-chip stability in a sector often buffeted by commodity volatility and capex cycles.

Our dividend policy is straightforward and disciplined: We target a payout ratio of 45-55% of adjusted EPS, with strong free cash flow coverage of at least 1.5x. In Q3, we generated $285 million in FCF—up 12% year-over-year—despite steel input costs rising 8% amid lingering supply chain disruptions from the Red Sea rerouting. This covered our $112 million quarterly dividend payout by 2.6x, and our full-year FCF payout coverage now stands at 1.8x. On an EPS basis, our trailing 12-month adjusted EPS of $6.15 supports a payout ratio of just 44%, leaving ample room for reinvestment while rewarding shareholders.

Historically, this policy has served us well. Over the past decade, we've grown our dividend at a 9% compound annual growth rate (CAGR), outpacing both inflation and the 6.5% CAGR for the broader Industrials Select Sector Index. This resilience shines through downturns—like the 2020 COVID capex freeze, when we still hiked 4%—driven by our diversified end-markets: 45% infrastructure and mining, 30% ag and forestry equipment akin to Deere's portfolio, and 25% factory automation systems competing with the likes of Fanuc and ABB.

Regionally, our dividend sustainability ties directly to these trends. In North America, which drove 52% of Q3 revenue, we're riding the tailwinds of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). Backlogs for our 777G-class haul trucks and battery-electric excavators—similar to Caterpillar's 793F autonomous models—stand at 18 months, fueled by $1.2 trillion in federal spending. This has boosted our U.S. utilization rates to 92%, supporting FCF yields north of 8%. Contrast that with EMEA, at 22% of sales, where energy crises and a 15% drop in German machinery orders have tempered growth; yet, our 2.1x dividend coverage there remains rock-solid, thanks to localized manufacturing in our Dortmund facility hedging Eurozone inflation.

In APAC, representing 26% of revenue, we're seeing robust demand from China's stimulus-driven renewables push and India's PLI scheme for manufacturing. Orders for our IoT-enabled predictive maintenance kits—integrated with Siemens MindSphere-like platforms—jumped 22% YoY, offsetting softer commodity exposure in Australia. These dynamics affirm our policy's balance: Dividends fund shareholder returns without compromising our $450 million FY24 capex plan, 60% of which targets technical initiatives like digital twins for hydraulic presses and Level 4 autonomy in wheel loaders, mirroring Komatsu's Frontier innovations.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on yield accretion through compounding growth. Our book value dividend coverage exceeds 65%, and with ROIC at 14.2%—top quartile versus peers like Cummins at 12%—we're positioned to sustain 7-9% annual dividend growth over the medium term. This assumes normalized steel prices ($750/ton HRC) and mid-single-digit revenue expansion from electrification megatrends; our EV-compatible powertrain modules already contribute 8% of backlog, with pilots at John Deere and Volvo CE.

Looking ahead, we expect to maintain this trajectory into 2025, targeting a forward yield north of 3.2% as shares trade toward our $105 fair value on improving EPS visibility. We're not chasing yield at the expense of growth—unlike some higher-yielding peers exposed to cyclical mining downturns—but delivering total returns blending 3% yield with 8-10% EPS growth.

In summary, our dividend policy underscores IndusEquip's fortress balance sheet and industry-tailored discipline. It's a promise kept through booms, busts, and everything in between.

As we turn to guidance, I'm pleased to share our outlook for operating margins in Q4 and the full fiscal year 2024. We continue to execute strongly on our margin expansion playbook amid a resilient industrial backdrop, driven by robust U.S. infrastructure spending, selective pricing discipline, and our accelerated push into high-margin digital services and aftermarket solutions.

First, a quick recap: In Q3, we delivered an operating margin of 14.2%, up 180 basis points year-over-year, reflecting a 220 bps gross margin expansion to 28.5% from improved mix—particularly our servo-driven CNC machining centers and IoT-enabled predictive maintenance contracts—and disciplined SG&A leverage at 8.1% of sales. This performance underscores the efficacy of our 'Smart Factory 2.0' initiative, which has yielded $45 million in annualized savings through AI-optimized supply chain routing and robotic process automation in our assembly lines.

Looking to Q4, we expect operating margins in the range of 14.5% to 15.2%, representing sequential expansion of 30 to 100 basis points. This guidance assumes total revenues of $1.45 billion to $1.50 billion, in line with our prior outlook, with organic growth of 5-7% driven by backlog conversion in our core segments: capital equipment (55% of mix), aftermarket parts (25%), and services/digital (20%).

Key drivers include gross margin tailwinds projected at 29.0-29.5%, bolstered by 2-3% targeted price realization on our hydraulic press brakes and automated welding systems, offsetting modestly higher steel and aluminum input costs (up ~4% QoQ due to lingering supply constraints from U.S. Midwest mills). Our fixed-price commodity hedges, covering 70% of FY25 needs, mitigate ~60% of this inflation. OpEx efficiency with SG&A at 7.8-8.0% of sales, down from Q3, via continued outsourcing of non-core logistics to partners like XPO Logistics and our new generative AI tools for demand forecasting, which have reduced inventory obsolescence by 15%. Regional dynamics: U.S. demand remains a bright spot, with IIJA-funded projects fueling 12% YoY growth in our earthmoving equipment line, akin to trends at Caterpillar. EMEA softens slightly to flat due to elevated energy costs impacting auto OEM capex (e.g., delayed orders from Volkswagen Group suppliers), while Asia-Pacific holds mid-single digits on strength in semiconductor fab tools despite China's uneven recovery. Mix shift: Aftermarket and digital services expected to contribute 22% of Q4 revenue, up from 18% last year, with 35%+ margins from our 'IndusEdge' platform—subscription-based predictive analytics using edge computing on our CNC lathes, mirroring Honeywell's Forge model.

For the full year FY2024, we now guide operating margins to 14.0% to 14.4%, an upward revision of 20 bps from our prior range, implying ~410 bps expansion versus FY2023's 9.9%. This tracks to full-year revenues of $5.75-5.85 billion, with adjusted operating income of $805-845 million. Year-to-date, we've realized $120 million in productivity gains from technical initiatives like digital twin simulations for our new electric forklift lineup (launching Q1 FY25, targeting 25% market share in warehouse automation) and supplier consolidation—reducing our vendor base by 20% while localizing 40% of North American steel sourcing to counter tariff risks.

Strategically, we're prioritizing three levers for sustained margin accretion into FY2025 and beyond: Industry 4.0 acceleration with $150 million capex in FY25 for brownfield upgrades, including 5G-enabled cobots from partners like Universal Robots, aiming for 2% annual COGS reduction; electrification and sustainability, where our Gen-3 battery-powered excavators, compliant with EU Stage V emissions, position us for green procurement wins, with services attach rates climbing to 40%; and share gains in high-growth verticals, targeting 15% penetration in EV battery gigafactory equipment (e.g., competing with Kuka Robotics) and aerospace MRO, where margins exceed 30%.

Of course, risks to this guidance include potential FX headwinds—a stronger USD could shave 20 bps if sustained—or softer-than-expected China fab spending amid U.S. export controls on advanced lithography tools. We're well-hedged, with 80% of exposures covered.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us on IndusEquip's Q3 earnings call. Today, I'd like to dive deep into one of our highest-growth areas: our automation and digital offerings portfolio, which continues to be a key driver of both top-line expansion and margin accretion. As you know, IndusEquip is a leader in industrial equipment for sectors like automotive, aerospace, and heavy machinery, and our pivot toward Industry 4.0 solutions—encompassing IIoT platforms, AI-enabled predictive maintenance, collaborative robotics, and digital twin technologies—has positioned us perfectly amid the global push for smart manufacturing.

Let me start with the numbers, which speak for themselves. In Q3, our automation and digital segment delivered $285 million in revenue, up 28% year-over-year and 12% quarter-over-quarter. This marks the ninth straight quarter of double-digit growth, outpacing the broader industrial automation market, which IDC pegs at around 15% CAGR through 2027. Recurring revenue from our software-as-a-service (SaaS) offerings, including our flagship IndusEdge AI platform and Predix-like asset performance management suite, hit $112 million—representing 45% of segment revenue and growing 42% YoY. Overall, digital services now account for 22% of total company revenue, up from 16% a year ago, with EBITDA margins expanding to 38% in the segment, compared to 32% last year. This high-margin profile is pulling our company-wide adjusted EBITDA margin up by 210 basis points to 24.5%.

What's fueling this growth? First, technical initiatives that are resonating with our OEM and end-user customers. We've rolled out version 3.0 of IndusEdge, our edge-computing platform that integrates NVIDIA Jetson Orin modules for real-time machine learning at the factory floor. This allows for sub-millisecond latency in anomaly detection—think vibration analysis on CNC machines or thermal imaging on welding robots—reducing unplanned downtime by up to 35%, based on pilots with customers like a major German automotive tier-1 supplier. We're also seeing strong uptake in our digital twin ecosystem, powered by partnerships with Siemens NX and Autodesk Forge, where we've deployed over 5,000 virtual replicas this quarter alone. These twins enable 'what-if' simulations for process optimization, boosting Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) from typical industry averages of 65-70% to over 85% in validated cases.

On the robotics front, our cobot lineup—similar to Universal Robots but scaled for heavy-duty applications—grew 32% YoY, driven by demand for human-machine collaboration in labor-short markets. We've integrated ROS2 (Robot Operating System) with our proprietary AI orchestration layer, allowing seamless fleet management across 50+ SKUs.

Now, turning to efficiency impacts, these offerings aren't just revenue generators; they're transforming customer economics and our own P&L. For customers, the value proposition is clear: our predictive maintenance algorithms, leveraging time-series data from over 1.2 million connected sensors across our installed base, have delivered $450 million in quantified customer savings YTD through reduced Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) by 28% and extended Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) by 22%. A real-world example: our deployment at a U.S. steel fabricator mirrored Emerson's AspenTech successes, cutting energy consumption by 18% via AI-optimized furnace controls, while improving throughput by 15%.

Internally, digital adoption has streamlined our operations. By applying our own IIoT stack to our factories in Monterrey and Suzhou, we've achieved a 14% reduction in scrap rates and 9% lower conversion costs quarter-over-quarter. This 'dogfooding' approach not only validates our tech but also accelerates R&D cycles—our time-to-market for new automation modules is now down to 9 months from 18.

Regionally, growth is broad-based but with bright spots. North America led at 35% YoY growth, fueled by reshoring trends under the CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act—think semiconductor fabs and EV battery plants snapping up our SCADA-integrated automation suites. EMEA grew 25%, with sustainability mandates like the EU's Green Deal driving demand for our energy-efficient digital twins; we've secured €150 million in backlog from wind turbine OEMs akin to Vestas. Asia-Pacific, our largest market, expanded 22%, tempered by softer Chinese capex but offset by 45% growth in India and Southeast Asia, where we're partnering with Foxconn-like assemblers for smart factory retrofits. Emerging markets now represent 18% of digital bookings, up from 12%.

Strategically, we're doubling down on servitization to capture more wallet share. Our 'Equipment-as-a-Service' (EaaS) model, blending hardware CAPEX with OPEX-based digital subscriptions, now has Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) of $420 million, with 95% gross retention rates. This shifts us from one-off box sales to lifetime value—average customer LTV has risen 40% to $2.5 million over 7 years. Looking ahead, we're targeting 30%+ segment growth in FY25, supported by $500 million in R&D investment focused on generative AI for autonomous orchestration and 5G private networks. Risks like cybersecurity—we've invested heavily in zero-trust architectures compliant with NIST 800-82—and supply chain volatility for semiconductors are on our radar, but our multi-sourcing with TSMC and GlobalFoundries mitigates this.

In summary, automation and digital are the flywheel for IndusEquip's transformation into a software-industrial hybrid, much like Rockwell's FactoryTalk evolution or ABB's Ability platform. This segment's momentum underscores our confidence in delivering 12-15% organic revenue growth and mid-20s EBITDA margins long-term.

Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call for IndusEquip Inc. Before we open the line for questions, I'd like to provide our forward-looking revenue guidance for the fourth quarter and full fiscal year 2024, along with the key drivers, regional breakdowns, and strategic context shaping our outlook. As always, these figures are based on our current visibility into end-market demand, order backlog, and macroeconomic trends, and they exclude any potential M&A activity beyond our recently closed acquisition of Precision Robotics Systems.

Starting with the headline numbers: For Q4, we are guiding revenue to $1.45 billion to $1.50 billion, representing sequential growth of 5% to 9% from Q3's $1.48 billion and year-over-year growth of 8% to 12%. This puts us on track for full-year 2024 revenue of $5.75 billion to $5.85 billion, a robust 11% to 14% increase over 2023's $5.20 billion. Organic growth—net of the 3% contribution from the PRS tuck-in—is expected to drive the majority at 8% to 10% for both the quarter and the year.

Let me break this down by the key levers. First, end-market demand remains resilient across our core segments. Discrete automation, which accounted for 42% of Q3 revenue, continues to outperform, fueled by semiconductor capital spending and AI data center buildouts. We're seeing strong pull-through on our next-gen collaborative robots—similar to Universal Robots' UR series but with our proprietary AI-vision integration—and wafer fab automation lines. Bookings in this segment grew 18% YoY in Q3, pushing our backlog to $4.2 billion, up 22% from year-ago levels, with visibility extending into mid-2025. We expect discrete automation to grow 15% to 18% in Q4, outpacing the segment's overall mid-teens expansion.

In our process equipment vertical—think CNC machining centers and precision grinders for aerospace and EV battery production—growth moderates to 7% to 10% YoY in Q4. Here, Boeing's ramp-up on 737 MAX and 787 programs, combined with North American OEMs like Tesla and GM investing in gigafactory expansions, is offsetting softer European auto demand amid their EV transition headwinds. Our multi-axis 5G-enabled CNCs, with sub-micron accuracy and real-time predictive maintenance via our IndusEdge IoT platform, are winning share; we've secured $450 million in new frame agreements with Tier-1 suppliers this quarter alone.

Construction and mining equipment, at 28% of the mix, faces the expected seasonal slowdown but still delivers flat to 3% growth. High interest rates are capping capex in non-residential construction, echoing Caterpillar's recent commentary on North American softness, but our backlog of $1.8 billion in hydraulic excavators and autonomous haulers provides a floor. Notably, our electrified skid-steers and battery-powered dozers—aligned with OSHA's emissions regs and customer ESG mandates—are gaining traction, with a 25% YoY increase in green equipment orders.

Pricing remains a tailwind, contributing 2% to 3% to top-line growth. We've successfully passed through 4.5% average price realization YTD on inflation-indexed contracts, particularly in aftermarket parts and services, which now represent 22% of revenue and grew 14% in Q3. Our service attachment rates hit 68%, up from 64% last year, driven by uptime guarantees on our connected fleet.

Regionally, the Americas will drive 60% of Q4 revenue, growing 12% to 15% YoY on reshoring tailwinds. The CHIPS Act is supercharging fab equipment demand—think Applied Materials-scale projects—and Mexico's nearshoring boom is boosting maquiladora orders for assembly line robotics. EMEA, at 25% of the mix, expects 5% to 8% growth, tempered by Germany's industrial slowdown and UK infrastructure delays, but offset by wind turbine nacelle tooling for Siemens Gamesa and Vestas. Asia-Pacific, 15% of revenue, accelerates to 10% to 13% with China reopening capex post-COVID lockdowns and India's PLI scheme fueling electronics manufacturing. FX headwinds—primarily a 2% USD strength—shave 1% off the year-over-year comps.

Strategically, we're leaning into Industry 4.0 and sustainability megatrends to sustain mid-teens organic growth into 2025. Our $250 million FY24 capex plan—up 15% YoY—targets capacity expansion at our Rockford, IL, and Monterrey facilities to 95% utilization by year-end, adding 20,000 units of annual robot output. We've launched IndusForge, our digital twin platform integrating Siemens MindSphere-like analytics with generative AI for 30% faster machine programming, which is already embedded in 40% of new orders. On the M&A front, PRS bolsters our software stack with ROS2-compatible middleware, targeting $100 million in synergies by 2025 through cross-selling into legacy installed bases.

Risks to this guidance include potential delays in customer capex—e.g., if Fed rate cuts are deferred beyond Q1—or supply chain flare-ups in rare earths for our permanent magnet motors. Conversely, upside could come from accelerated AI infrastructure spend or our pending DOE grants for clean energy equipment. We see adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 150 to 200 bps to 22.5% to 23% for the year on operating leverage.
